questions.q: What data would hurt most if it were encrypted or deleted tomorrow?
questions.why: Points straight at the buckets that need immutability first.
questions.need: The data that would hurt most is known and protected first
questions.how: Name it with the business, and protect it first
questions.listen: Backups and records under legal hold usually top the list; they set the level of protection.
questions.probe: Which of that data has a legal retention period?

questions.q: What do you pay today per terabyte, including egress and requests?
questions.why: Request and egress fees are where storage bills surprise people.
questions.need: The full cost per terabyte is known
questions.how: Add up storage, egress and requests for a typical month
questions.listen: Charges for retrieval and requests often double the headline price.
questions.probe: What did retrieving data cost the last time you restored from the cloud?

questions.q: Which applications and backup jobs write to object storage, and where?
questions.why: Unknown writers mean unknown tenants and keys.
questions.need: Every application and backup job writing to object storage is known
questions.listen: Each application that writes is a compatibility test for the proof.
questions.probe: Which of them use more than simple reads and writes: versioning, lifecycle rules, notifications?

questions.q: Do you know how many access keys exist, who owns them and when they were last used?
questions.why: Old keys with broad rights are the easiest way in.
questions.need: Every access key has an owner and is used
questions.how: Review keys, give owners, and remove unused ones
questions.listen: Old keys with broad rights are a common way in.
questions.probe: When was a key last rotated, and what broke?

questions.q: Are your backup copies under object lock, and for how long?
questions.why: Backups an administrator can delete do not survive ransomware.
questions.need: Backup copies are under object lock for long enough
questions.how: Turn on object lock with the agreed retention
questions.listen: Backups that can be deleted with the right keys can be deleted by an attacker.
questions.probe: Which lock mode is used: one even administrators cannot override, or one they can?

questions.q: Must any data stay in a given country, and can you prove where it is?
questions.why: Residency is often a legal requirement before it is a technical one.
questions.need: Data that must stay in a country stays there, with proof
questions.how: Pin buckets to regions and keep the evidence
questions.listen: Being able to prove where data is matters as much as where it is.
questions.probe: Who would ask for that proof: a regulator, a customer, an auditor?

questions.q: When did you last restore from these backups, and how long did it take?
questions.why: The restore is the only test that counts.
questions.need: A restore from object storage has been tested and timed
questions.how: Restore one backup end to end and time it
questions.listen: Restore speed depends on throughput, not capacity: measure it.
questions.probe: How long would restoring the largest system from these copies take?

questions.q: Who is alerted when someone reads or deletes far more than usual?
questions.why: Mass reads and deletes are the first signs of theft or ransomware.
questions.need: Unusual reads or deletes alert someone named
questions.how: Alert on unusual volumes, routed to an owner
questions.listen: Mass reads can mean theft; mass deletes can mean an attack.
questions.probe: Who can stop a key from working within minutes?

questions.q: How much data will be stored, in how many objects, and how much is written each day?
questions.why: Capacity, object count and daily writes size the platform.
questions.need: Capacity, object count and daily writes are estimated
questions.how: Collect current size and daily writes per bucket or application
questions.listen: Billions of small objects stress metadata more than capacity: ask about object size too.
questions.probe: What is the typical object size, and the largest?

questions.q: How fast must data be written and read back, in the backup window and during a restore?
questions.why: Throughput, not capacity, decides backup and restore times.
questions.need: The throughput needed for backup and restore is known
questions.how: Divide the size of the backup set by its window to get the throughput needed
questions.listen: A nightly window and a restore target give a throughput the design must meet.
questions.probe: What is the restore time target for the largest backup set?

questions.q: Which data should move to cheaper storage, or be deleted, automatically as it ages?
questions.why: Lifecycle rules keep cost down without anyone acting.
questions.need: Lifecycle and retention rules are agreed per data set
questions.how: Agree tiering and expiry per bucket with its owner
questions.listen: Data kept forever by default is the cost to cut: give each rule an owner.
questions.probe: Which data set has no retention rule at all today?

questions.q: Do analytics or AI teams need to read this data where it is, and with which tools?
questions.why: Data read in place avoids copies and transfer charges.
questions.need: Needs to read data in place for analytics or AI are known
questions.how: Ask the data teams which tools and protocols they would read with
questions.listen: Reading in place turns a backup target into a data platform: a strong second use.
questions.probe: How much data is copied today only to be analysed elsewhere?

questions.q: Will the storage serve several teams or customers, each seeing only its own data and usage?
questions.why: Serving several tenants needs isolation, quotas and usage per tenant.
questions.need: Tenants, quotas and usage reporting are agreed
questions.how: List the teams or customers and what each must see
questions.listen: Charging back per team needs usage per tenant from the first day.
questions.probe: How is the cost of storage split between teams today?

questions.q: How would you know if a bucket were open to the internet, and who checks?
questions.why: An open bucket is one of the most common ways data leaks.
questions.need: No bucket is open to the internet by mistake, and a change that opens one is caught
questions.how: List the buckets that are public on purpose, and alert on any other that becomes public
questions.listen: A list of the public ones and an alert; "nobody would do that" is what every leak report starts with.
questions.probe: Which buckets are public on purpose today, and who decided?
